candidate.title: Keep score: name, change, trace and debug

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Distinguish a variable's name, current value and an instruction that changes its value.
Without the worked example, explain: Trace ordered scoring instructions, distinguishing replacement from adding to the current value.

pedagogy.rationale: Model a named store with cards, then build and trace scoring procedures. Test predictions against a partner's trace, repair initialization errors and transfer the procedure to a different game.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Read whole numbers to twenty, with oral support if needed.
Add small whole numbers and follow ordered instructions.

misconceptions.description: The variable's name is changed whenever its number changes.
misconceptions.response: Keep the name score fixed and replace the number stored beneath it.

misconceptions.description: Set score to a number is treated as adding that number.
misconceptions.response: Set replaces the current value. Add uses the current value to calculate the next one.

misconceptions.description: Initialization is repeated before every event, discarding the accumulated score.
misconceptions.response: Initialize at new-game start and retain the updated value between events.

misconceptions.description: A set instruction is ignored and the previous value is retained.
misconceptions.response: Follow every instruction in order. Set replaces the old value even if no points were earned.

misconceptions.description: A new game starts without initialization and inherits an earlier game's score.
misconceptions.response: Give each new game its stated starting value before processing events.

scenes.title: Predict before playing
scenes.learnerAction: Write a prediction and explain what must be remembered between the two turns.

content.body: Our class invents a paper target game. Each hit earns two points. A scorekeeper must remember the total between turns. Start at zero. Predict the score after two hits before moving counters. This game is an invented teaching example.

prompts.prompt: Predict the score after two hits. Explain what the scorekeeper must remember between turns.

scenes.title: A name stays; its value changes
scenes.learnerAction: Make a name card and a separate number card. Sort the examples, then explain their different jobs.

content.body: Write score above a space on paper. Put a number card beneath it. The name identifies the store. Its current value is the number there now. An instruction tells the scorekeeper what to do. After a hit, change the number card; keep the name.

accessibility.textAlternative: Write score above a space on paper. Put a number card beneath it. The name identifies the store. Its current value is the number there now. An instruction tells the scorekeeper what to do. After a hit, change the number card; keep the name. Sort the name, the number and the instruction. Groups: Variable name, Current value, Instruction. Cards: score, 4, Add 2 to score, Set score to 1.

offline.note: Use the printed text, diagrams and questions with paper and pencil. Responses can be spoken and scribed.

blocks.prompt: Sort the name, the number and the instruction.

cards.why: This label names the store, regardless of its current number.
This number can be stored under the name score.
This tells the scorekeeper how to change the stored number.
This replaces the stored number with 1; it is not another name.

scenes.title: Trace one instruction at a time
scenes.learnerAction: Copy a three-column table: instruction, value before, value after. Move the number card after each instruction.

content.body: A trace records each instruction and its result. Set score to 0 gives 0. Add 2 gives 2; add 2 again gives 4. Set score to 1 replaces 4 with 1. Add 2 now gives 3. Setting and adding do different jobs. Order matters because each instruction uses the current state.

hints: Keep score as the label in every row.
For set, replace the old number. For add, start with the current number.

accessibility.textAlternative: A trace records each instruction and its result. Set score to 0 gives 0. Add 2 gives 2; add 2 again gives 4. Set score to 1 replaces 4 with 1. Add 2 now gives 3. Setting and adding do different jobs. Order matters because each instruction uses the current state. How does each instruction change score? Step 1: New game: set score to 0. There is no earlier game value to reuse. Step 2: Add 2: 0 becomes 2. Add 2 again: 2 becomes 4. Step 3: Set score to 1: 4 becomes 1, rather than 5. Step 4: Add 2: 1 becomes 3. The variable is still named score.

steps.text: New game: set score to 0. There is no earlier game value to reuse.

scenes.title: Build a trace with help
scenes.learnerAction: Build the instruction cards, trace them and check both decisions.

content.body: Use a new game that starts with one point. A hit adds three points. Follow two hits, then a card saying set score to 2. Record every new value. Point to the current number before following each instruction. Explain whether the last instruction adds or replaces.

hints: After each hit, add three to the number currently under score.
The final card says set to 2. It replaces the old number with 2.

accessibility.textAlternative: Use a new game that starts with one point. A hit adds three points. Follow two hits, then a card saying set score to 2. Record every new value. Point to the current number before following each instruction. Explain whether the last instruction adds or replaces. The value changes from 1 to 4. What happens to the variable name? Options: It stays score.; It becomes four.; It needs both score and four as names.. After the two hits, set score to 2. What is its new value? Options: 7; 2; 9.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to labelled controls and response fields. Use Enter to check an attempt. An oral response may be dictated or scribed.

items.prompt: The value changes from 1 to 4. What happens to the variable name?

options.feedback: The name identifies the same store while its content changes.
Four is the new value, not a new name for the store.

options.text: It needs both score and four as names.
options.feedback: One name can hold different values over time.

items.prompt: After the two hits, set score to 2. What is its new value?

options.feedback: Seven was the value before the set instruction. The instruction changes it.
Set to 2 replaces the current value with 2.
Nine comes from adding 2 to 7. The instruction says set, not add.

scenes.title: Decide when to initialize
scenes.learnerAction: Choose where initialization belongs, then use the cards to explain two hits in one game.

content.body: Initialization gives a variable its starting value. Place a new-game card before the event cards. Keep the score between turns. A new game needs a fresh start, even when the previous game ended with a score. Ask a partner to follow your cards literally.

hints: Ask whether another turn is a new game.
Reset once when a new game begins; use the retained score for later turns.

accessibility.textAlternative: Initialization gives a variable its starting value. Place a new-game card before the event cards. Keep the score between turns. A new game needs a fresh start, even when the previous game ended with a score. Ask a partner to follow your cards literally. Where should set score to 0 go? Options: Never, even when another game starts.; Once at the start of each new game.; Before every hit..

items.prompt: Where should set score to 0 go?

options.text: Never, even when another game starts.
options.feedback: Without initialization, an old game's score can carry into a new game.

options.text: Once at the start of each new game.
options.feedback: This creates a fresh game while retaining points between its turns.
That erases earlier points, so two hits can look like one hit.

scenes.title: Repair the procedure, then retest
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose the bug, change the cards and explain the retest results.

content.body: A fictional scorekeeper resets the score before every hit. Two hits still produce only two points. A bug is a mistake in instructions or their order. Identify the instruction that loses information. Repair the procedure, then test it with three hits and with a separate new game.

prompts.prompt: Show the repaired cards and traces for three hits and a separate new game. Explain why changing the points per hit would not fix the reset bug.

answerGuidance.prediction: Two hits give4 from an initial0. Require an explanation that the previous value is retained.
answerGuidance.model: The worked trace is0,2,4,1,3. The variable name stays score.
answerGuidance.guided: Starting1, two additions of3 give4 then7; set to2 gives2, not9. Initialization belongs at each new game's start.
answerGuidance.independent: Initial2, hit5, hit8, reset1, hit4. A complete trace records the initial state and each event, not only the final answer.
answerGuidance.tests: Separate new games: no events gives2; one hit gives5; reset then hit gives4. Accept other well-defined learner tests with correct predictions. A hit then reset gives1, demonstrating that order can change the result.
answerGuidance.debug: Move initialization outside the repeated event procedure. Three hits from0 give2,4,6; a separate game starts again at0. Increasing the award to4 merely masks the error for one event count.
answerGuidance.transfer: Accept coherent new rules with named state, explicit initialization, an increase and replacement. Require two traces and evidence-based revision or justification. Do not prefill a claim that a partner test occurred.

segments.activity: Separate name, value and instruction using cards
Model replacement versus addition with a trace

teacherGuide.materials: Paper name/value/instruction cards, counters or drawn marks, pencil. No device or interpreter required.
teacherGuide.support: Read instructions aloud. A pupil may direct a partner or scribe who moves cards and records their decisions. Model before/after columns during guided work only. Keep independent traces unscaffolded.
teacherGuide.extension: Compare add-then-set with set-then-add. Explain when two event sequences produce different scores and create a counterexample to a claimed rule.
teacherGuide.oversight: Check the full state trace, reasons for set versus add, chosen boundary tests and actual repair. Choice success alone is insufficient evidence of the performance task.
teacherGuide.assessment: Formative practice only. No governed assessment, mastery attribution or official score. Independent assessment requires separately governed items.
teacherGuide.offline: Print scene text and cards. Use oral or written trace explanations. Do not require dragging, color, fast reading or precise motor control.
teacherGuide.retention: Propose a different scoring procedure after7 days, including initialization and replacement. No retrieval job is scheduled here.

expectedTraces.review: Require each intermediate state and its explanation. Correctness on one trace is not a mastery claim. Accept coherent learner games with their own stated rules.

lessons.paper:
Keep score: name, change, trace and debug

Predict before playing

Our class invents a paper target game. Each hit earns two points. A scorekeeper must remember the total between turns. Start at zero. Predict the score after two hits before moving counters. This game is an invented teaching example. Predict the score after two hits. Explain what the scorekeeper must remember between turns.

Predict the score after two hits. Explain what the scorekeeper must remember between turns.
Response: __________________________

A name stays; its value changes

Write score above a space on paper. Put a number card beneath it. The name identifies the store. Its current value is the number there now. An instruction tells the scorekeeper what to do. After a hit, change the number card; keep the name. Sort the name, the number and the instruction. Groups: Variable name, Current value, Instruction. Cards: score, 4, Add 2 to score, Set score to 1.

Trace one instruction at a time

A trace records each instruction and its result. Set score to 0 gives 0. Add 2 gives 2; add 2 again gives 4. Set score to 1 replaces 4 with 1. Add 2 now gives 3. Setting and adding do different jobs. Order matters because each instruction uses the current state. How does each instruction change score? Step 1: New game: set score to 0. There is no earlier game value to reuse. Step 2: Add 2: 0 becomes 2. Add 2 again: 2 becomes 4. Step 3: Set score to 1: 4 becomes 1, rather than 5. Step 4: Add 2: 1 becomes 3. The variable is still named score.

Keep score as the label in every row.

For set, replace the old number. For add, start with the current number.

Build a trace with help

Use a new game that starts with one point. A hit adds three points. Follow two hits, then a card saying set score to 2. Record every new value. Point to the current number before following each instruction. Explain whether the last instruction adds or replaces. The value changes from 1 to 4. What happens to the variable name? Options: It stays score.; It becomes four.; It needs both score and four as names.. After the two hits, set score to 2. What is its new value? Options: 7; 2; 9.

After each hit, add three to the number currently under score.

The final card says set to 2. It replaces the old number with 2.

Decide when to initialize

Initialization gives a variable its starting value. Place a new-game card before the event cards. Keep the score between turns. A new game needs a fresh start, even when the previous game ended with a score. Ask a partner to follow your cards literally. Where should set score to 0 go? Options: Never, even when another game starts.; Once at the start of each new game.; Before every hit..

Ask whether another turn is a new game.

Reset once when a new game begins; use the retained score for later turns.

Build and trace a fresh game

Work independently. A new game starts at two points. A hit adds three points. A reset event sets score to one. Follow hit, hit, reset, hit. Write the starting value and a row for each event. Explain what one row tells another scorekeeper. Record the initial value and every later value for hit, hit, reset, hit. Explain the reset row and keep the variable name visible.

Record the initial value and every later value for hit, hit, reset, hit. Explain the reset row and keep the variable name visible.
Response: __________________________

Choose tests that could expose a mistake

Test your procedure with no events, one hit and a hit after a reset. Predict each result before your partner follows the cards. Start each separate test as a new game. Compare predictions with the trace. A match is evidence for that case, not proof that every possible case works. For each test, show the event sequence, predicted value and observed trace. Add a different test and explain what mistake it could reveal.

For each test, show the event sequence, predicted value and observed trace. Add a different test and explain what mistake it could reveal.
Response: __________________________

Repair the procedure, then retest

A fictional scorekeeper resets the score before every hit. Two hits still produce only two points. A bug is a mistake in instructions or their order. Identify the instruction that loses information. Repair the procedure, then test it with three hits and with a separate new game. A new game starts at zero; each hit should add two points. A fictional scorekeeper wrote: Before each hit: set score to 0. After each hit: add 2 to score. After two hits, report 2. Which repair preserves earlier points? Options: Move set score to 0 to the new-game start, before all turns.; Rename score to total after every hit.; Keep resetting but add 4 after each hit.. Show the repaired cards and traces for three hits and a separate new game. Explain why changing the points per hit would not fix the reset bug.

Show the repaired cards and traces for three hits and a separate new game. Explain why changing the points per hit would not fix the reset bug.
Response: __________________________

Make a game someone else can follow

Invent a target game for classmates using paper tokens. Choose a starting score, an increase and an event that replaces the score. Write precise instructions. Ask a partner to follow them without extra explanations. Use their trace to find an unclear instruction or justify why a test matched. Present your game cards and two traces with a changed event order. Explain one revision or a test-based reason for keeping an instruction. What stayed the same when the variable's value changed?

Present your game cards and two traces with a changed event order. Explain one revision or a test-based reason for keeping an instruction. What stayed the same when the variable's value changed?
